opus-5.5.text:
So, there's a real trade-off here, and I don't think either one has fully won yet.

With a depth transformer, you keep everything in the discrete token world. You take your audio codec, say something with residual vector quantization producing several codebooks per frame, and you have a big temporal transformer moving across time, plus a small transformer that predicts the codebooks within each frame. It's very natural if you come from language modeling: you have a single cross-entropy loss, you can sample with temperature, and it plugs neatly into a text backbone. It's also easy to make streaming, which matters a lot for real-time voice. The downside is that you're bound by the quality of your quantizer. If the codec loses information, you can't get it back. And the more codebooks you add for fidelity, the more sequential steps you pay at inference.

Flow matching goes the other way. You model continuous latents directly, so you avoid quantization artifacts and can often get better acoustic quality, especially for prosody and fine detail. Sampling can also be quite efficient if you use a small number of integration steps. But it fits less naturally into an autoregressive, token-by-token setup. You need to think carefully about how to condition it, how to make it causal and streaming, and how to mix it with a language model that's predicting discrete text.

In practice, what seems to work well is a hybrid: let the autoregressive backbone handle semantics and timing, the "what to say and when," and use something like a flow-matching head per frame for the acoustic details. You get the controllability and streaming of the autoregressive model, and the fidelity of continuous generation.

So it depends on what you're optimizing for. If you want a simple, robust system that's tightly integrated with a text LLM, the depth transformer is very attractive. If you care most about audio quality and you're willing to deal with a bit more engineering complexity, flow matching becomes really compelling. My guess is that over time we'll see more of these hybrids rather than one approach completely replacing the other.

r001.rationale: The response says flow matching can sample efficiently with few integration steps, while adding codec codebooks increases the depth transformer's sequential inference steps.

r002.rationale: The response mentions using a small number of integration steps, but does not state that flow matching could support single-step inference.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't see them as competing on the same axis, which is why the question is a bit of a trap. A depth transformer is an architectural choice about how you factorize the token stream. Flow matching is a choice about how you model the continuous distribution of acoustic features. You can use both in the same system, and a lot of the better speech models now do.

Let me unpack what each one is actually buying you. In the depth transformer setup, you have a big temporal transformer that moves along the time axis, one step per frame, and then a small transformer that runs "vertically" at each frame to predict the hierarchy of codec tokens, from the semantic token down to the fine acoustic codebooks. The point is that you keep the expensive model at a low frame rate, say twelve and a half hertz, and let the cheap model deal with the eight or sixteen codebooks per frame. That solves a sequence-length problem and a dependency problem at once, because the codebooks within a frame are strongly correlated and you want to model them autoregressively rather than independently. It is very natural for streaming and for full-duplex, because the time axis is causal and you can interleave text and audio and even two speakers in the same stream.

Flow matching is attacking a different thing. Discrete codec tokens throw away information, and the more you compress to keep the temporal model small, the more you lose. Flow matching lets you model continuous representations, mel spectrograms or latents of a neural codec, directly. You get very high fidelity, and the training signal is clean. The cost is that most flow matching systems are non-causal and need the whole utterance, or at least a large chunk, and they need multiple sampling steps at inference. That is fine for text to speech where you have the transcript in advance. It is much harder for a conversational model that has to react within two hundred milliseconds.

So the way I weigh it is, what is the system supposed to do. If the product is high-quality offline synthesis or voice cloning, flow matching on continuous features is extremely strong and arguably simpler to train. If the product is a model that listens and talks at the same time, that has to be a language model at heart, and the depth transformer over discrete tokens is the design that makes the LLM part tractable. And the pragmatic answer is often the hybrid: a transformer predicts the coarse tokens or a continuous latent causally, and a flow matching decoder refines it in small chunks. You get back most of the fidelity without giving up the streaming behavior.

One more thing I would say. People sometimes argue about this as if the audio modeling were the hard part. It is not anymore. The hard part is keeping the model smart. The moment you train a language model on audio tokens, you tend to lose reasoning and knowledge compared to the text model it started from. The inner monologue trick, aligning text tokens with the audio stream so the model is still "thinking in text", matters more for quality of the conversation than whether the acoustic path is discrete or continuous. So I would push people to spend their effort there, and treat the depth transformer versus flow matching choice as engineering, decided by latency and by what you want the model to be.

r001.rationale: The response says flow matching needs multiple sampling steps, but does not state that it reduces sequential inference steps relative to an autoregressive depth transformer.

r002.rationale: The response does not say flow matching could support single-step inference.

astra-6.text:
I think they address somewhat different questions. A depth transformer is useful when you represent speech with several discrete codes per time step: you model how those codes depend on one another without making the temporal sequence much longer. Flow matching gives you a way to model continuous representations, which is attractive for capturing the variability in speech.

The tradeoff I would look at is quality versus inference cost and latency. With a depth transformer, you have sequential predictions across the codes. With flow matching, you typically have multiple refinement steps. Neither is automatically cheaper; it depends on how many steps you need and how you organize generation.

For a conversational system, I’d care particularly about how quickly you can produce the first chunk and whether you can keep generating smoothly. So I wouldn’t choose purely on the modeling objective. I’d compare them with similar representations and compute budgets, and measure intelligibility, expressiveness, and streaming latency. You can also combine the ideas; they aren’t necessarily mutually exclusive.

r002.rationale: The response says flow matching typically uses multiple refinement steps and does not mention that it could support single-step inference.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they address somewhat different parts of the problem. A depth transformer is a natural way to model the dependencies between the different codebooks of a speech tokenizer. You can use a temporal transformer to model how speech evolves over time, and then a smaller transformer to generate the codes within each time step. The tradeoff is that those predictions introduce sequential work, which matters when you want low latency.

With flow matching, you can model continuous acoustic representations and generate a whole group of values together. But you typically need several steps to produce a sample, so parallel generation doesn’t automatically mean faster generation.

For me, the comparison has to be end to end: at the same latency and compute budget, which gives you better speech quality, intelligibility, and expressiveness? Especially for a conversation, I’d care about how quickly you can start speaking and whether you can keep streaming. I wouldn’t assume either approach wins independently of the representation and the inference setup.
